title: An element is a unit exactly when its class modulo a locally nilpotent ideal is a unit

standard_prerequisites.name: Local nilpotence of an ideal
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: The hypothesis on I, used at proof lines 6510-6511
standard_prerequisites.use: Gives z^N = 0 for each element z of the ideal, which is what terminates the geometric series argument.

standard_prerequisites.name: Congruence modulo a principal ideal
standard_prerequisites.use: Lets the identity xy = 1 - z be read as 1 congruent to z modulo xR, so that x divides 1.

core_obligations: One direction is immediate: the image of a unit in R/I is a unit (proof line 6505).
For the converse, take y with xy = 1 - z for some z in I, and read the identity as 1 congruent to z modulo the principal ideal generated by x (proof lines 6507-6509).
Use local nilpotence to get z^N = 0, raise the congruence to the N-th power to get 1 congruent to 0 modulo xR, and conclude that x divides 1 and is a unit (proof lines 6510-6513).
proof_roadmap: Reduce to showing that some multiple of x equals 1 (proof lines 6504-6508).
Use nilpotence of the discrepancy to kill it by taking a high power of the congruence (proof lines 6509-6513).
difficulty_reason: For a ring R with a locally nilpotent ideal I, the lemma states that an element x is a unit exactly when its class in R/I is a unit (statement lines 6496-6502). The proof does not use lifting of units along a nilpotent extension in the abstract: from a class y with xy = 1 - z and z in I it reads the identity as 1 congruent to z modulo the principal ideal generated by x, uses that z is nilpotent, raises the congruence to a high power to obtain 1 congruent to 0 modulo xR, and concludes that x divides 1 (proof lines 6504-6514). Turning nilpotence into the termination of a geometric-series style argument is the substance, and the author writes it out. H2.
